history.text: Hey, I'm Flow — I'll be taking your interview today. Please start with a short introduction.

Hi Flow, I'm Priya Raman. I have eight years of experience in backend engineering, currently serving as a tech lead for a payments platform in a fintech company. My expertise lies in Go, Postgres, Kafka, and AWS. I recently led a successful migration from a monolithic architecture to microservices, which resulted in a 40% reduction in p99 latency. I also take pride in mentoring two junior engineers. Prior to this role, I worked at a logistics startup that was acquired. I’m excited to discuss how my background and skills can contribute to your team.
Got it. You mentioned leading a migration to microservices. What were the biggest challenges you faced during that process?

During the migration to microservices, one of the biggest challenges was managing inter-service communication effectively. We had to ensure that services were loosely coupled while maintaining performance. I also encountered resistance from some team members who were accustomed to the monolithic approach, which required clear communication about the benefits. To address these challenges, I organized workshops to educate the team on microservices best practices and implemented a phased migration plan. This approach minimized downtime and allowed for thorough testing at each stage, ultimately leading to a successful transition.

You organized workshops to educate the team on best practices. Tell me about a time when you had to deliver a complex backend solution under a tight deadline. How did you ensure that you met the project requirements while maintaining high standards?
[stage_change -> behavioral_q1]

In my previous role at a logistics startup, we faced a situation where we needed to deliver a complex shipping optimization feature within a two-week deadline due to a new client requirement. To ensure we met the project requirements while maintaining high standards, I implemented a sprint approach. I broke down the task into smaller, manageable components and prioritized essential features based on client needs. I conducted daily stand-ups to track progress and addressed roadblocks immediately. By leveraging existing libraries and frameworks, we were able to speed up development. We delivered the feature on time, and it resulted in a 25% increase in operational efficiency for our client.
You broke down the task into smaller components. What specific challenges did you face while prioritizing those essential features?

One specific challenge in prioritizing the essential features was balancing the client’s immediate needs against the long-term scalability of the solution. The client wanted quick fixes that addressed short-term pain points, but I knew that some of those might lead to technical debt. To tackle this, I facilitated discussions with the client and the team to align on priorities. We used a value-versus-effort matrix to identify which features would deliver the most significant impact with manageable complexity. This approach not only helped us stay focused on what mattered but also ensured that we built a sustainable foundation for future enhancements.

You facilitated discussions to align on priorities. Describe a situation where you identified a significant inefficiency in a backend process. What steps did you take to simplify or improve it, and what was the impact?
[stage_change -> behavioral_q2]

In my current role, I identified a significant inefficiency in our payments processing system, where transactions were being delayed due to synchronous calls to external services. I took the initiative to analyze the flow and discovered that these calls were the bottleneck, especially during peak times. To improve this, I proposed transitioning to an asynchronous processing model using Kafka for message queuing. I led a small team to implement this change, ensuring we maintained data integrity through careful design. The result was a 50% reduction in transaction processing time, which significantly enhanced user experience and contributed to a higher retention rate among our customers.
You led a small team to implement the change. How did you ensure the team was aligned and effectively communicated throughout the transition to the asynchronous model?

To ensure alignment and effective communication during the transition, I set up a dedicated Slack channel for real-time updates and discussions related to the project. I also established regular check-in meetings to review progress and address any roadblocks. At the outset, we agreed on clear goals and responsibilities, which helped everyone understand their roles. Additionally, I encouraged an open feedback culture where team members could voice concerns or suggest improvements. This transparency fostered collaboration and kept everyone aligned, ultimately leading to a smoother transition and successful implementation of the asynchronous model.

You established regular check-in meetings to review progress. Tell me about a time when you had to disagree with a team member or stakeholder regarding a technical decision. How did you handle the situation, and what was the final outcome?
[stage_change -> behavioral_q3]

In a recent project, I disagreed with a stakeholder who favored implementing a third-party API for payment processing. I believed it would introduce unnecessary dependency and potential risks, especially regarding latency and compliance. To handle the situation, I requested a one-on-one meeting to discuss my concerns. I presented data on our historical transaction failures with similar APIs and outlined alternative solutions that would give us more control and stability. We ultimately agreed to develop an in-house solution that leveraged our existing infrastructure. This decision not only mitigated risks but also improved our processing speed by 30%, which proved beneficial in the long run.
You presented data on historical transaction failures with similar APIs. What specific data or examples did you use to support your argument during that discussion?

During the discussion, I presented specific metrics showing that previous integrations with third-party APIs had a failure rate of approximately 15%, primarily due to latency issues that spiked during peak traffic times. I also shared examples from our incident logs, highlighting instances where customers experienced delays that led to chargebacks. Additionally, I included a comparison of response times between the third-party service and our internal capabilities, illustrating that our in-house solution consistently performed faster. This data helped underline the risks and potential financial impact, making a compelling case for opting for a more controlled approach.

Thanks, Priya. The part about "This transparency fostered collaboration and kept everyone aligned, ultimately leading…" is the kind of specific that lands. Your written feedback is on your dashboard in a minute. That's the end of the interview — take care.
[stage_change -> closing]
